items.stem: What is the purpose of a handoff between agents in an orchestrated workflow?

options.text: To pass a request to a more suitable specialised agent to continue the work
options.rationale: Correct: a handoff routes work to the agent best suited to it.
A handoff transfers work; it does not erase history.

options.text: To switch to a cheaper billing plan
options.rationale: Handoffs are about routing, not billing.

items.stem: When is a single-agent design preferable to multiple agents?

options.text: When the task is cohesive and multiple agents would add needless complexity
options.rationale: Correct: use the simplest design that meets the need; extra agents add overhead.

options.text: Always, because multiple agents never work
options.rationale: Multiple agents are valuable for genuinely distinct responsibilities.

options.text: Never, because more agents is always better
options.rationale: More agents is not inherently better and can add complexity.

options.text: Only when the newest model is used
options.rationale: Model version does not decide single vs multi-agent design.

items.stem: Which TWO controls should be in place before releasing an orchestrated multi-agent workflow? (Select TWO)

options.text: Tracing so each step and handoff can be diagnosed
options.rationale: Correct: tracing is essential to understand and debug orchestrated runs.

options.text: Tests that verify requests route to the correct agent
options.rationale: Correct: routing/handoff tests confirm the orchestration behaves as designed.

options.text: Removing all guardrails to simplify the flow
Letting any agent perform any action
options.rationale: Unbounded agent actions undermine safety and scope control.
